editorial_contributions.text: Let \(\chi\) denote the chromatic number of the unit distance graph of the plane. It is known that \(4\leq\chi\leq 7\) but it is a long outstanding problem to determine \(\chi\). The authors motivate that \(\chi\) may depend upon the system of axioms we choose for set theory. So they give an example of graph \(G\) with chromatic number 2 assuming the axiom of choice and with chromatic number greater \(\omega\) working in a model with the countable axiom of choice and such that every set of real numbers is Lebesgue measurable (LM). Further on they have the following conditional theorem: Assume that any finite distance graph has chromatic number 4. Then assuming the axiom of choice, the chromatic number of the plane is 4. Assuming dependent choice and LM, the chromatic number of the plane is 5, 6 or 7.

title.title: Chromatic numbers of the plane. III: Its future

editorial_contributions.text:
This very nicely presented book, lovingly prepared by the author over a period of 18 years, studies problems involving colored objects, and the Ramsey theory that such problems are imbedded into. Two problems receiving special attention are the well-known four color problem (resolved in 1976 after an assault of 124 years) and the author's ``favorite open problem in mathematics'', the chromatic number of the plane problem: What is the smallest number of colors sufficient for coloring the plane so that no two points of the same color are unit distance apart? The book is very thorough, in unusual ways perhaps best expressed by the author himself: 


 
``This book includes not just mathematics, but also the process of investigation, trains of mathematical thought, and where possible, psychology of mathematical invention. The book does not just include history and prehistory of Ramsey theory and related fields, but also conveys the process of historical investigation -- the kitchen of historical research if you will. It has captivated me, and made me feel like a Sherlock Holmes -- I hope my reader will enjoy this sense of suspense and discovery as much as I have. \dots I hope the book will present mathematics as a human endeavor: the reader should expect to find in it not only results, but also portraits of their creators; not only mathematical facts, but also open problems; not only new mathematical research, but also new historical investigations; not only mathematical aspirations, but also moral dilemmas of the times between and during the two horrific World Wars of the twentieth century.''


 
For example, new facts and artifacts are presented, pertaining to the lives of Issai Schur, Pierre Joseph Henry Baudet, and Bartel Leendert van der Waerden. The 49 chapters are divided into 11 parts: I. Merry-go-round; II. Colored plane; III. Coloring graphs; IV. Coloring maps (a map is defined to be a plane connected multigraph with no bridges); V. Colored graphs; VI. The Ramsey principle; VII. Colored integers: Ramsey theory before Ramsey and its aftermath; VIII. Colored polygons: Euclidean Ramsey theory; IX. Colored integers in service of chromatic number of the plane; X. Predicting the future (here the author conjectures that the chromatic number of the plane is either 4 or 7, expressing a preference for 7); XI. Farewell to the reader. There are an extensive bibliography, and indices of names, subjects, and notations; the latter two are brief. The author has used his own book as a text, at both the senior and the graduate level. There are numerous open problems, but no formal problem sets. But there is much to recommend this book, both for mathematicians and for those who wish to learn more about mathematicians and their subject.

editorial_contributions.text:
This book is addressed to lower undergraduate students and presents the 20-year account of the Colorado Mathematical Olympiad. The volume under review contains original problems with complete solutions.

The content of this volume is divided into four main parts, as follows:

Part I contains the problems posed in the first ten years of competition, namely from 1984 to 1993. 

Part II: Further explorations; Rooks in space; Chromatic number of the plane; Polygons in a colored circle, polyhedra in a colored sphere; How does one cut a triangle?; Points in convex figures; Triangles in a colored plane; Rectangles in a colored plane; Colored polygons; Infinite-finite; Schur theorem. 

Part III contains the problems posed in the second decade of competition, namely from 1994 to 2003.

Part IV: Further explorations; Chromatic number of a grid; Stone Age entertainment; The Erdős problem; Squares in a square; Washington recangles; Olde Victorian map colouring; More Stone Age entertainment; The 1-10-100 problem; King Arthur and the knights of the round table; A map coloring ``game''.

The book under review is a collection of interesting and fresh problems with detailed solutions. Soifer's treatment is colloquial and could be used for general classroom enrichment as well as for competition preparation. This reviewer warmly recommends this book as an introduction to problem solving and the construction of proofs.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: First László Székely [\textit{L. Szekely}, ``Measurable chromatic number of geometric graphs and sets without some distances in Euclidean space,'' Combinatorica 4, 213--218 (1984; Zbl 0558.05020)] and more recently Saharon Shelah and Alexander Soifer [\textit{S. Shelah} and \textit{A. Soifer}, ``Axiom of choice and chromatic number of the plane,'' J. Comb. Theory, Ser. A 103, No.\,2, 387--391 (2003; Zbl 1030.03035)] have presented examples of infinite graphs whose chromatic numbers depend on the axioms chosen for set theory. The existence of such graphs may be relevant to the Chromatic Number of the Plane problem. In this paper we construct a new class of graphs with ambiguous chromatic number. They are unit distance graphs with vertex set Rn, and hence may be seen as further evidence that the chromatic number of the plane might depend on set theory.

editorial_contributions.text:
Chromatic graph theory deals with coloring vertices, edges, or both of a graph \(G\) according to certain simple rules. However, the simplicity of the rules does not mean that the problems encountered are simple. Starting from the four-color problem around 1850, the theory has developed into a many-sided body of problems, theories, results, and applications. The number of simply stated but challenging problems remains large and growing.

The author's Mathematical coloring book (TMCB) was published in 2009 [The mathematical coloring book. Mathematics of coloring and the colorful life of its creators. Forewords by Branko Grünbaum, Peter D. Johnson jun., and Cecil Rousseau. New York, NY: Springer (2009; Zbl 1221.05001)]. It is now joined by the New mathematical coloring book (TNMCB), which is a colossal sibling of TMCB. This second edition of the book is a masterpiece, containing more than twice as much as the first edition. It includes striking results from the past fifteen years and solutions to problems from the first edition.

This very nicely presented book studies problems involving colored objects and the Ramsey theory. It mainly deals with the four-color problem and the author's favorite problem, namely, the chromatic number of the plane problem: What is the smallest number of colors needed for coloring the points of the plane in such a way that any two points at distance one receive two different colors? This book includes not just mathematics, but also the process of investigation. It is a unique combination of mathematics, history, and biography and the author has been intimately involved in the story for the last half-century. Mathematics is presented both as science and art and the author has set a standard for writing about mathematics and mathematicians that will be hard to match. The author engages the reader's attention not only mathematically, but emotionally and esthetically.

TNMCB consists of 68 chapters divided into 14 parts. I. Merry-go-round; II. Colored plane; III. Coloring graphs; IV. Coloring maps; V. Colored graphs; VI. The Ramsey principles; VII. Colored integers: Ramsey theory before Ramsey and its aftermath; VIII. Colored polygons: Euclidean Ramsey theory; IX. Colored integers in service of the chromatic number of the plane: how O'Donnell unified Ramsey theory and no one noticed; X. Ask what your computer can do for you XI. What about chromatic 6?; XII. Predicting the future; XIII. Imagining the real and realizing the imaginary; XIV. Farewell to the reader.

A large part of this new edition presents the most recent works by Auberg de Grey, Marijn Heule, Jann Parts, Geoffrey Exoo, and Don Ismailescu. New open problems and conjectures are included and this will lead to further work on the theme of this book. This book is strongly recommended to all those who wish to learn more about mathematics, mathematicians, the process of investigation and the psychology of mathematical invention.

title.title: On the chromatic number of the plane for map-type colorings

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: The Hadwiger-Nelson problem asks for the minimum number of colors required to color the plane such that if two points are unit distance apart from each other, then those points have different colors \textit{H. T. Croft} et al. [Unsolved problems in geometry. New York etc.: Springer-Verlag (1991; Zbl 0748.52001)]. It has been shown that the chromatic number of the Euclidean plane is 5, 6, or 7 (see [H. T. Croft, loc. cit.] and [\textit{A. De Grey}, ``The chromatic number of the plane is at least 5'', Preprint, \url{arXiv:1804.02385}]). Versions of this problem for the hyperbolic plane are investigated in [\textit{E. De Corte} and \textit{K. Golubev}, ``Lower bounds for the measurable chromatic number of the hyperbolic plane'', Preprint, \url{arXiv:1708.01081}] and [\textit{H. Parlier} and \textit{C. Petit}, ``Chromatic numbers for the hyperbolic plane and discrete analogs'', Preprint, \url{arXiv:1701.08648}]. In this paper, we answer this question for the Taxicab plane. In particular, we show that the minimum number of colors necessary to color the Taxicab plane such that no two points unit distance apart have the same color is four. We do this by tiling the plane using taxicab circles, all of which have radius \(r=1/2\). All the points in the interior of a given circle are colored using the same color. However, the interiors of adjacent circles are colored using different colors, and the boundary of each circle is colored using all four of the colors. This is done in such a way that points on opposite sides of a circle are colored using different colors.
